name: Çifte Minareli Medrese
desc: A 13th-century Seljuk college whose brick twin minarets and deeply undercut stone portal face straight down Erzurum's main street. The courtyard is open to the sky, so snow sits in it half the year, and the domed Hatuniye tomb at the back is the quietest corner. Three conical Saltuqid tombs stand two minutes south.
season: May–Oct; Dec–Mar the courtyard is under snow and the stone is punishing to touch
tip: Walk two minutes south to the Üç Kümbetler — three conical tombs on a patch of grass that almost every coach party skips.
rev: Visitors call the portal carving the finest Seljuk stonework outside Divriği, while grumbling that half the building is usually behind restoration hoarding and there is almost no signage in English.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, 12 km out; the medrese sits on Cumhuriyet Caddesi and everything downtown is walkable

name: Yakutiye Medrese
desc: Built in 1310 under Ilkhanid rule, this one is roofed rather than open, which matters in Erzurum. The surviving minaret is sheathed in turquoise and dark blue tile, and the facade carries palm trees, lions and a double-headed eagle. Inside is the city's Turkish-Islamic arts museum, with local kilims and silver oltu-stone work.
season: Year-round — it is one of the few Erzurum sights that works in a January blizzard
tip: The oltu-stone workshops in the covered bazaar behind it cut the black jet into rosaries while you wait, and prices drop sharply once you leave the street facing the medrese.
rev: Reviewers like that it is warm, compact and genuinely museum-like, but several note the collection is thin for the ticket and that the second minaret has been missing for centuries despite the name.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then any city bus or a 15-minute taxi to Cumhuriyet Caddesi

name: Palandöken
desc: A bare, treeless ridge rising straight off the southern edge of Erzurum, with the top station above 3,100 m and long fall-line runs that drop back towards the city lights. The snow is dry and cold because of the altitude, and the Ejder run is one of the longest continuous descents in the country.
season: Dec–Mar for skiing; summer is dull grassy slopes and an empty gondola
tip: Stay in the city rather than the slope hotels — a taxi to the lifts costs less than a single resort dinner and you get to eat in real kebab houses.
rev: Skiers rate the snow quality and near-empty pistes highly, but the recurring complaints are old lifts, brutal wind that shuts the upper chairs, and very little après-ski beyond hotel lobbies.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 20 minutes by road to the lift base; free hotel shuttles run in season

name: Tortum Waterfall and Lake
desc: A landslide dammed the Tortum river centuries ago, creating a long green-blue lake that ends in a 48 m fall crashing into a rock bowl. Below the drop the spray keeps a patch of forest permanently wet. The lake road north towards Uzundere runs through orchards and poplar rows with the water on one side the whole way.
season: May–Jul when the hydro plant releases enough water; by September the fall can be a trickle
tip: Water is diverted to the power station most of the year, so ring the Uzundere tourism office before driving up — the fall runs hard mainly in late spring.
todo: Stairs down to the plunge pool
rev: When the water is on, people call it the most impressive fall in the east; when it is off, reviews turn bitter about a long drive to a dry cliff and a car park full of tea stalls.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then about 100 km north on the Artvin road; buses to Yusufeli pass the junction

name: Narman Fairy Chimneys
desc: Cappadocia in rust red: eroded pinnacles and fluted ridges of iron-rich sandstone spread across a valley the locals call the Red City. There are no cave churches and no balloons, just raw geology, sheep tracks and a light that turns the whole amphitheatre orange in the last hour of the day.
season: May–Oct; the access track is mud or snow from November
tip: Go in the late afternoon and walk into the bowl rather than shooting from the roadside platform — the scale only registers when a shepherd walks past the pinnacles.
rev: Those who make the drive report having the place entirely to themselves, but many warn the last few kilometres are unsurfaced, badly signposted and impassable for a low car after rain.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then roughly 100 km northeast via Oltu road; you need your own vehicle

name: Pasinler
desc: A black basalt castle on a cone above a farming town, built by the Saltuqids and fought over by Ottomans and Russians ever since. The climb takes twenty minutes and gives you the whole Pasin plain, one of the great grain basins of the east. Down in town there are sulphur baths fed by a hot spring.
season: Apr–Oct for the castle; the thermal baths make sense even in deep winter
tip: Do the castle first and the hamam second — the Hasankale thermal pools are hot, cheap, and full of farmers rather than tourists.
rev: People rate the view and the near-total absence of other visitors, while noting the castle interior is largely rubble, the path is loose underfoot, and the thermal facilities are basic and men-only in places.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 40 km east on the Ağrı road; minibuses leave from Erzurum's Gölbaşı terminal

name: Cağ Kebabı
desc: Lamb stacked on a horizontal spit over wood embers, cut into skewers as the outside crisps, then handed to you to slide onto flatbread with raw onion and sumac. It started in Oltu and Erzurum turned it into a lunchtime institution. Ordering is by the skewer and the counter keeps a running count.
season: Year-round; a plate of it after a January morning outside is the point
tip: Eat it before two in the afternoon — the good places carve one spit a day and simply close when the meat runs out.
rev: Almost universally praised as the best lamb in Türkiye, with the caveats that the per-skewer bill climbs faster than people expect and that the famous places are cramped, smoky and cash-preferred.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then a short taxi to the centre; the cluster of grills is around Cumhuriyet Caddesi

name: Kemaliye (Eğin)
desc: Old Ottoman houses with carved wooden ceilings stacked on a shelf above the Euphrates, built with money sent home by emigrants. Above the town runs the Taş Yolu, a road hacked through cliff by hand over decades, running in and out of raw rock tunnels with the river a long way below.
season: May–Oct; the Taş Yolu tunnels are unlit and the gorge road is grim in winter
tip: Drive the Taş Yolu from the Kemaliye end towards Dutluca early in the morning — the tunnels are single-lane, and meeting a tractor in one is not fun.
rev: Travellers describe it as the most spectacular road in Anatolia and the town as genuinely lived-in, but warn about no barriers, falling rock, and hotel beds that vanish entirely on summer weekends.
onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then about 140 km southwest; the last stretch from İliç is slow and winding

name: Girlevik Waterfall
desc: Water spills over a wide travertine lip in dozens of separate threads rather than one column, dropping into a wooded gorge below Çağlayan village. In February the whole face freezes into a curtain of ice that draws climbers from across the region. In summer it is a picnic spot with tea gardens on the terraces.
season: Apr–Jun at full flow; late Jan–Feb for the frozen face
tip: Carry on 3 km past the falls to the Girlevik ice cave and the upper springs — nearly everyone stops at the first tea garden and turns around.
rev: Consistently called worth the detour, though visitors complain the picnic area is littered on summer weekends and the loud music from the tea gardens carries right to the base of the falls.
onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then roughly 30 km southeast via Çağlayan; minibuses run in summer only

name: Ergan Mountain
desc: The ridge that hangs directly over Erzincan, with a gondola from the edge of town lifting you to about 2,600 m in a quarter of an hour. In winter it is a small, cheap ski hill with wide-open north-facing bowls; in summer the top is meadow, crocus and a view straight down onto the Erzincan plain.
season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for the meadows and the ride up
tip: Ride the gondola even without skis — the return ticket is trivial and the top station terrace is the best table in Erzincan on a clear evening.
rev: Locals rate the value and the short transfer from town, but reviews mention that the gondola is often shut for wind or maintenance and that the resort has almost no infrastructure once you are up there.
onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, 10 km away; the gondola base is on the southern edge of the city

name: Altıntepe
desc: An Urartian hill fort on a low mound beside the Erzincan–Erzurum highway, excavated to reveal a temple, a columned audience hall and rock-cut tombs that gave up gold and bronze now in Ankara. What survives on site is foundations and a fine view, but it is one of the westernmost Urartian outposts and almost nobody stops.
season: Apr–Oct; the mound is exposed and there is no shade or shelter
tip: See the finds first in the Erzincan museum, otherwise the site reads as a field of stone outlines with no explanation.
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find it rewarding for its scale and isolation, but general reviews are lukewarm: little signage, an unstaffed gate, and everything portable removed to museums.
onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then 20 km east on the D100 towards Üzümlü; the mound is signposted off the highway

name: Ani
desc: A dead medieval capital on a grass plateau that ends at a gorge, with the Armenian border on the far bank. Red and black tufa churches stand alone in the wind — the cathedral by Trdat, the round church of the Redeemer sheared in half by lightning, and Tigran Honents with its frescoes still readable. The silence is the main thing.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; wind on the plateau is relentless and July midday is fierce
tip: Take the far loop to the Tigran Honents church and the gorge edge first, before the coaches arrive around eleven and cluster near the cathedral.
todo: Church of St Gregory of Tigran Honents
Gorge edge and the ruined bridge
rev: Repeatedly described as one of the most moving ruins anywhere, with the standard complaints of no shade, a long exposed circuit, patchy restoration work and a site that closes earlier than people expect.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then 45 km east by taxi or the morning minibus from Kars centre; no food at the site

name: Kars Castle and the Russian Quarter
desc: Below the castle rock, Kars is laid out on a grid of grey basalt houses with pedimented windows, built during forty years of Russian rule and looking nothing like the rest of Türkiye. The castle itself is a short steep walk with the Kars river, an old stone bridge and a domed bathhouse at its foot.
season: May–Oct; Jan–Feb is genuinely arctic but the snowbound streets are the atmosphere Pamuk wrote about
tip: Start at the Kümbet Mosque — a 10th-century Armenian church of the Holy Apostles with carved apostles round the drum — then follow the river up to the castle.
rev: Visitors enjoy the odd Baltic-looking streets and the castle view over the plateau, but note the castle interior is empty, many old houses are derelict, and the town shuts down early and completely.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, 6 km out; the whole old town is walkable and the castle is 20 minutes uphill from the centre

name: Lake Çıldır
desc: A shallow high lake at 1,960 m that freezes solid for months. In deep winter fishermen cut holes in the metre-thick ice and pull out carp, and villagers run horse-drawn sleds across the surface with sheepskins over your knees. In summer it is a plain blue lake with geese, storks and very few visitors.
season: Jan–Feb for ice and sleds; Jun–Sep for birds and the ring road
tip: Ice thickness is checked daily by the sled men — go on a weekday and negotiate directly at Doğruyol village rather than booking through a Kars hotel.
todo: Grilled carp at a lakeside shack
rev: The winter sled ride draws delighted reports, tempered by warnings about aggressive touting on the ice, prices that triple at weekends, and thin summer visits when there is little to do but drive round.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then about 45 km northeast; tours from Kars combine it with Ani in one long day

name: Sarıkamış
desc: Rare crystal snow falls on one of the largest Scots pine forests in the world, and the pistes run between the trees rather than above them — unusual in Türkiye. The town below still has tsarist barracks and the memorial to the ninety thousand Ottoman soldiers who froze here in the winter of 1914.
season: Late Dec–Mar for snow; Jun–Sep for forest walks and cold clear nights
tip: Ski the tree runs on the Cıbıltepe side in the morning and drive up to the Allahuekber memorial in the afternoon — the forest road there is the most beautiful part of the district.
todo: Walk in the Scots pine forest
rev: Skiers praise the dry powder and empty slopes, but complain that lift capacity is small, the hotel scene is limited to a handful of resorts, and the town itself offers very little in the evening.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then 55 km southwest by road; the Doğu Ekspresi also stops in Sarıkamış
